opus-5.5.text:
I think they're related but not the same thing, and people often conflate them.

Long context is, in a sense, a mechanism. You make the window bigger, so the model can attend to more tokens at once. That's very useful, and it has improved a lot. But long-term memory is more of a capability, or even a property of a system: can an agent accumulate experience over time, and does that experience actually change how it behaves later?

One way to see the difference: if I give you a million tokens of everything you've ever done, that's not the same as you having learned from it. Humans don't remember by replaying their whole life every morning. We compress, abstract, forget most things, and keep what matters. Some of it becomes explicit knowledge, some becomes intuition or habit. So memory involves selection and transformation, not just storage.

There are roughly three ways to approach it today. One is to just extend the context, which is simple and general but expensive, and attention over a huge context isn't always reliable. Another is external memory, like retrieval or files the agent writes and reads. That's practical, and a lot of agents already work this way, but the agent has to know what to write down and when to look it up. The third is putting it into the weights, some form of continual learning, which is the most "human-like" but also the hardest, because you face forgetting, stability, and safety issues.

My guess is the real answer will be some combination. Long context is like working memory: it gets bigger and more powerful. But for an agent that works with you for months, or that operates in a company across many tasks, you need something beyond the window. That's where I think a lot of the interesting research is: not just "how long can the context be," but "how does the system decide what's worth remembering, and how does that make it better over time." In a way, it's tied to the bigger question of how agents can learn from their own experience, rather than only from pretraining data.

r001.rationale: The response lists extending the context window as one approach to long-term memory, describing it as a way to include more tokens at once.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're related but not the same thing, and it's worth separating them.

Long context is about what you can fit into a single forward pass, essentially the working memory of the model. Long-term memory is about what persists across interactions, across episodes, across time, and that has to live somewhere outside the context window, as weights, as files, as some retrieval store. So in a sense long context is a necessary ingredient but it's not sufficient. Even if you had a million tokens, or ten million, you still face a question that long context alone doesn't answer: what goes in, and what gets left out.

Humans are actually an interesting reference point here. Our working memory is tiny, famously something like seven items, and yet we function pretty well over decades, because we have very good mechanisms for compression, for forgetting, for deciding what's worth encoding. So I don't think the right framing is "make context infinitely long and the memory problem disappears." The harder and more interesting problem is the management layer: how does an agent decide what to write down, what to summarize, what to retrieve, and when. That's a learning problem, not just an architecture problem.

The way I've been thinking about it in agent work, like with ReAct or with language agents more broadly, is that memory is really part of the action space. Reading from and writing to memory are actions the agent takes, and you can train those just like you train any other decision. Longer context makes the agent more forgiving of bad memory decisions, because it can afford to carry more around. But if you want an agent that works for months on a task, or learns from thousands of past episodes, you can't just carry everything. You need the agent to learn what matters.

So my short answer is: long context expands the bandwidth of short-term memory, and that's genuinely useful, but long-term memory is a different capability that's more about judgment than capacity. And I actually think the frontier right now is less about pushing the context number and more about letting models learn, through experience, how to use whatever memory they have.

r001.rationale: The response says long context expands short-term memory and is not sufficient to solve long-term memory. It does not identify sufficiently long context as a possible implementation of long-term memory.

astra-6.text:
我觉得这两个概念有联系，但不是一回事。长上下文解决的是：模型在一次思考的时候，能够看到多少信息。长期记忆解决的是：在很多次交互之后，哪些信息应该留下来，以及以后什么时候、以什么形式把它们拿出来用。

比如你跟一个助手聊了一年，即使上下文窗口足够大，可以把这一年的聊天记录都放进去，也不代表它就有了很好的记忆。它还需要判断，哪些是你的长期偏好，哪些只是当时随口说的话，哪些信息已经发生了变化。记忆不只是存储，还包括筛选、更新，甚至遗忘。

所以我更倾向于把长上下文看成长期记忆的一种基础能力。窗口越大，系统就越容易把相关的历史信息带进来，不一定需要非常激进地压缩。但你仍然需要一套机制，决定带什么进来。否则，每次都重新读一遍所有历史，成本很高，也未必能抓住重点。

反过来，长期记忆也不一定只能通过上下文实现。你可以把信息存在外部，通过检索拿回来；也可以把某些经验变成更稳定的策略，甚至通过学习进入模型参数。关键是，过去的经验能不能持续改善未来的行为。

所以我觉得它们更多是互补关系。长上下文让模型当下能处理更多东西，长期记忆让模型跨越不同的任务和时间，能够积累经验。真正好的助手，应该既能读懂你现在给它的材料，也能记住过去跟你合作时学到的东西。

r001.rationale: The response describes long context as a foundational capability for long-term memory, allowing relevant history to be brought into the current context.

sol-6.1.text:
我觉得这两个概念有关系，但不完全是一回事。Long context 更多是在说，模型在某一次处理信息的时候，能看到多少东西；long-term memory 则是在说，一个系统在长期运行的过程中，怎么保留过去的经验，并在未来合适的时候使用它们。

比如我们今天聊了两个小时，你可以把整个对话都放进 context 里，这当然是一种实现记忆的方式。但如果我们聊了一年，可能就不能简单地把所有东西不断往里面塞。你需要决定哪些信息值得留下，哪些可以压缩，以及什么时候把什么信息找回来。这里面不仅有存储的问题，还有学习和管理的问题。

所以 long context 会让做 memory 更容易，也会改变我们设计 memory 的方式。以前可能需要很细地切分、检索，现在可以一次给模型更多背景。但 context 越长，并不自动意味着记忆越好。模型能不能从大量信息里面找到真正相关的东西，能不能区分已经过时的信息和新的信息，这些仍然是问题。

我更倾向于把 long context 看成一种基础能力，把 long-term memory 看成建立在这些能力之上的系统机制。最终重要的不是它记住了多少，而是过去的经历能不能让它下一次做得更好。

r001.rationale: The response says that putting an entire conversation into the context is one way to implement memory, clearly presenting long context as a possible memory mechanism.
